title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 14
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The First Technology
passages.text:
A. Cooking is so ordinary that its significance is easy to miss. No other animal does it, every human society does, and the difference it makes is not merely one of taste. Heat breaks down structures in plant and animal tissue that digestion would otherwise have to break down, so a cooked meal delivers more usable energy for less digestive work than the same food raw. The proposal that this mattered evolutionarily is now taken seriously, though the details remain contested.

B. The anatomical evidence is suggestive rather than decisive. Compared with other primates of similar size, humans have small teeth, weak jaws, a short gut and a large, expensive brain. Each of these is consistent with a diet requiring less mechanical and chemical processing, and the combination is difficult to explain without some form of external food preparation. What the anatomy cannot establish is when the change occurred or whether cooking specifically, rather than pounding or fermenting, was responsible.

C. Dating controlled fire is the central difficulty and the reason the debate persists. Fire leaves traces that resemble the traces of natural fire, and distinguishing a hearth from a burnt patch requires context that rarely survives. Claims for early control rest on sites where burnt material occurs in patterns hard to explain naturally, and each such claim has been contested by specialists arguing for alternative processes. The honest position is that the earliest secure evidence is considerably younger than the earliest proposed evidence.

D. A separate line of argument concerns time. Great apes of comparable body size spend a very large share of their waking hours chewing, and humans spend a small fraction of that. Whatever released those hours made them available for other activity, and the release is substantial enough that explanations not involving food processing struggle to account for it. This argument does not depend on dating fire, which is why it has held up better than the archaeological claims.

E. The social consequences may be as important as the nutritional ones. Cooking requires a delay between acquiring food and eating it, and a delay creates the opportunity for sharing, for theft and therefore for the arrangements that regulate both. A cooking group is a group that must tolerate waiting together around a resource that cannot be consumed immediately, and several researchers have argued that this is a more plausible origin for durable food-sharing arrangements than any account based on hunting success alone.

F. The counter-arguments deserve their weight. Populations documented eating largely raw diets exist, though they typically rely on processing that is not cooking and on food supplies that are unusually rich. Digestive gains from cooking vary substantially by food type, and the strongest effects are on starchy plants rather than on meat, which complicates accounts placing meat at the centre. The proposition that cooking mattered is well supported; the proposition that it was the single trigger for human distinctiveness is not.

passages.title: The Material That Does Not Go Away
passages.text:
Plastics are a family rather than a substance, and treating them as one is the source of much confusion in public discussion. The properties that make a food wrapper useful are not those that make a pipe or a surgical implant useful, and the disposal characteristics differ correspondingly. What the family shares is a resistance to the biological processes that break down other materials, because the molecular structures involved are not ones that organisms evolved to dismantle.

That resistance is a designed property and not a defect. A material intended to contain liquid, resist grease, exclude oxygen and survive handling must be stable, and stability against the environment is the same property as stability against decay. Criticism that treats persistence as a failure of engineering misunderstands the specification: the material was required to last, and it does.

What happens to plastic in the environment is fragmentation rather than degradation. Sunlight and mechanical abrasion break items into progressively smaller pieces without altering the underlying molecules, producing particles that pass through filtration, disperse widely and are now found in essentially every environment sampled, including places with no local source. This ubiquity is established. What those particles do at the concentrations actually observed is much less clear, and the gap between demonstrated presence and demonstrated harm is where most overstatement occurs in both directions.

Recycling has been oversold in a specific and consequential way. Mechanical recycling degrades polymer chains, so recycled material is generally of lower grade than the original and can substitute for it only in less demanding applications. This means recycling delays disposal rather than closing a loop, and the widespread public belief that plastic circulates indefinitely has reduced pressure for the interventions that do reduce volume. Sorting is also expensive and depends on a market for the output that has frequently not existed.

Substitution carries costs that comparisons often omit. Alternatives to plastic packaging are usually heavier, which raises transport emissions, and frequently less effective at preventing spoilage, which raises food waste — and the environmental cost of wasted food commonly exceeds that of the packaging that would have prevented it. Life-cycle assessments comparing materials therefore produce results that depend heavily on the assumptions made about waste rates, and single-figure comparisons should be treated with suspicion.

The interventions with the best evidence are unfashionable. Reducing unnecessary packaging, designing products for a single polymer type so that sorting is feasible, and building reuse systems for containers all reduce volume measurably. None generates the public engagement that beach cleaning does, and the mismatch between where attention goes and where measured effect lies is one of the more striking features of the field.

passages.title: Waiting as a Price
passages.text:
When a good is offered below the price that would clear the market, demand exceeds supply and something other than money must determine who receives it. Frequently that something is time: people queue, and the queue rations the good. This arrangement is common, is usually adopted for reasons of fairness, and has properties that are worth examining before it is assumed to be fair.

The first property is that queueing is not costless. The time spent has value, and it is a real cost borne by the person waiting — but unlike a price it is destroyed rather than transferred. A payment goes to the seller and can be spent; an hour in a queue benefits nobody. Rationing by waiting therefore consumes resources in the act of allocating, which is a defect no amount of good intention removes.

The second property is that it allocates to those with the lowest value of time rather than to those with the greatest need, and these coincide only sometimes. A person who is unemployed, retired or able to send someone else can outwait a person working two jobs, and the distributional outcome is not obviously more equitable than the one a price would produce — merely different, and less visible. Where the good is genuinely essential the outcome can be perverse.

Systems designed to be fair often reintroduce price through a secondary channel. Where queueing confers a valuable position, positions become tradable: people are paid to stand in line, appointments are resold, and intermediaries emerge to convert waiting into money. Prohibiting this is difficult, since the transaction is hard to observe, and its existence indicates that the underlying scarcity has not been removed by refusing to price it.

Alternatives exist and each carries its own difficulty. Lotteries allocate without consuming time, but discard information about who values the good most and are resented as arbitrary. Administrative allocation by assessed need can target better, at the cost of the assessment itself, which is expensive, intrusive and error-prone. Pricing with targeted transfers is the economist's usual proposal and is politically fragile, because it makes the allocation mechanism explicit in a way that queues do not.

What the analysis supports is narrower than either side usually claims. Queues are not inherently unjust, and they are not free; they impose a real and invisible cost, they favour a particular group, and they tend to generate the market they were adopted to avoid. Choosing among rationing mechanisms is a choice about which unfairness to accept, and arrangements presented as avoiding the choice have usually made it implicitly.
